taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO as Aristolochia serpentaria L. Several older segregate or varietal names are treated as synonyms in current references.
look_here_first: Start low on the plant, near the lowest nodes and leaf litter. The strange brown-purple flower has no ordinary petal whorl: the showy structure is a bent, tubular petaloid calyx/perianth. Then confirm the variable lanceolate-to-cordate leaves and the nearly spherical dry capsule.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — Purola Preserve natural flora documents Aristolochia serpentaria as naturally occurring in north Hays County. Travis — University of Texas Plant Resources Center Travis County Aristolochiaceae specimen index includes A. serpentaria. Kerr — Kerr Wildlife Management Area vascular flora documents A. serpentaria.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Only exact target-zone locality/county evidence was counted. Statewide Texas native status alone was not converted into county evidence.

best_field_traits: rhizomatous perennial herb, often inconspicuous in woodland litter
leaves variable from lanceolate to heart-shaped
flowers solitary on slender scaly peduncles from low nodes
petals absent; showy structure is a tubular S-shaped petaloid calyx/perianth
perianth brownish purple, enlarged basally and distally, with an unevenly three-lobed tip
dry nearly spherical capsule with numerous seeds
morphology_keys.family_training: Use A. serpentaria to teach that Aristolochia's bizarre flower is not a normal corolla. The perianth/calyx tube, inferior ovary, low flower position and capsule matter more than leaf shape alone.
morphology_keys.ecology: Moist to mesic woodland and shaded calcareous sites in Central Texas; larval host for pipevine swallowtail.

confused_with: other low woodland herbs when not flowering
comparisons.key_distinctions: A. serpentaria is a taller woodland herb with broader variable leaves and brown-purple low flowers; A. erecta is much shorter and grasslike with narrow leaves in sunnier/sandy sites. Use flower/perianth architecture and habitat rather than leaf shape alone.
